overview: Buganda grew around the Kabaka, chiefs and clans in the Lake Victoria region. Its history can also be read in barkcloth workshops, the wooden architecture of Kasubi and recordings of court musicians. Royal government changed under colonial rule and was later abolished; Baganda cultural life and a restored royal institution continue.

periods.title: Palace, burial place and royal craftsmanship
periods.summary: Kasubi was built as a royal palace in 1882 and became a burial place in 1884. Its arrangement of courtyard, gateway and thatched buildings joined architectural skill with royal ritual.

periods.title: A council within a changing political order
periods.summary: The 1900 Buganda Agreement formalized the Lukiiko within British indirect rule. Its later history included the negotiations associated with Kabaka Muteesa II's return from exile in 1955.

periods.title: Royal institutions suppressed
periods.summary: The palace attack in 1966 scattered musicians. The 1967 constitution abolished kingship and applied that abolition retrospectively to Buganda from May 1966. Cultural knowledge survived through people, objects and recordings.

periods.title: A restored cultural institution
periods.summary: The Kabaka and Lukiiko returned in 1993 with a cultural role. Musicians, craftspeople and caretakers continue traditions while also repairing losses and adapting their work for new generations.

items.text: Kasubi's palace became a royal burial ground in 1884. The main building, Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, used a circular plan, a domed thatched roof and wooden supports. Monumental architecture here depended on skilled work with plant materials, rather than masonry.

The documented interior combined palm-frond structural rings with long poles wrapped in barkcloth. A drum house and gatehouse faced the courtyard. These details connect construction, textile work and ceremonial movement within one royal compound.

After the destructive 2010 fire, restoration drew on surviving building knowledge as well as documentation. Kasubi left UNESCO's danger list in 2023. Conservation work announced in 2026 addresses disaster preparation, site management and community participation.

Craftspeople harvest the Mutuba tree's inner bark in the wet season and beat it with wooden mallets. Working under an open shed keeps it from drying too quickly. Repeated skilled handling produces a soft sheet from bark, without weaving threads.

Barkcloth served as bedding, curtains, storage material and clothing as well as ceremonial dress. Its household uses place the craft within ordinary work and comfort, alongside the royal and funerary settings in which it remains especially visible.

UNESCO identifies Ngonge clan craftspeople and a hereditary chief craftsman as custodians of this knowledge. Imported cotton reduced demand during the nineteenth century. Continued ceremonial use and later promotion helped sustain skills through a changing textile economy.

The 2021 album Buganda Royal Music Revival places archival sessions beside recordings made in 2017. Its credits name recordists and dates, allowing listeners to distinguish historical documentation from later performances rather than treating all tracks as one ancient sound.

The collection includes the endongo lyre, the large akadinda xylophone and an entenga ensemble of tuned drums. These are different approaches to melody, resonance and ensemble coordination, not interchangeable examples of drumming.

Performers credited include lyre player Albert Bisaso Ssempeke and royal harpist Temutewo Mukasa. Naming musicians preserves individual artistic work within a court tradition too often described only through kings and ceremonies.

The Lukiiko developed from advisory councils of chiefs and clan heads. Its organization changed during the nineteenth century and under the 1900 agreement. Its present cultural and consultative role should not be projected unchanged onto earlier royal government.

Article 118 of Uganda's 1967 constitution explicitly abolished royal offices. For Buganda it made that provision effective from 24 May 1966. This distinction explains why histories mention both years when describing the suppression of the kingdom.

ending.text: Buganda's royal political institutions were suppressed during the 1966 crisis and the constitutional changes of 1967. Their restoration in 1993 established a cultural role within Uganda. Baganda communities, crafts and music continued across that interruption; the map's final snapshot is not their disappearance.
